name: Carlos Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union or government, and what you say stays confidential: your name never goes with your answers. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on the early shift at a metal stamping plant out on the ring road, so the alarm goes at quarter to five and I'm clocked in by six. I run a line of big presses, the main one is 400 tonnes, that punch and bend steel coil into brackets and side panels for washing machines. Most of the day I'm feeding coil, watching the parts come off, checking them against the gauge and stopping the line when something looks wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's real. At two o'clock there's a pallet of parts that wasn't there at six, and I made that. What wears me out is the die changes when they go wrong, eight hours on concrete, and the new managers who arrive every two years with a fresh idea from a slide show. Pete, the setter I work with, has been there thirty years and he's watched every one of them come and go.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Lucía, she's a dental nurse, in a flat my brother and I bought together a few years back. We're careful with money. I've got over a year's pay put away, because my dad always said keep a year in the bank and you sleep fine. Sundays it's church with my mum and then football with the lads from the parish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one sounds about right to me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say already: it's mostly talk. The office lot get a new program that writes their emails, and down on the floor the presses still need someone to feed them and listen to them. I wouldn't post anything about it, I don't really go online for that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. I've got a good wage for an operator, a year saved, and plenty of other plants within twenty minutes if mine ever closed. If AI is mostly hype, my biggest worry is still my back at forty, not a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep doing my shifts, keep putting about a fifth of my pay in the savings account, and maybe in a year or two Lucía and I would look at a place of our own instead of half a flat with my brother. I'm not going to go and learn some AI program nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Monday, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned other plants nearby. Has your plant had a scare before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago we lost a fridge contract to a plant abroad and they cut the night shift. Nobody on days lost their job, and the lads from nights went to the car parts place down the road and were fine, because somebody's always hiring. That's the kind of worry I mean, and it's got nothing to do with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if Pete asked whether you'd stay thirty years like him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him maybe, if the presses keep running. Pete's got a house paid off and a pension from the old company, and that came from staying put. I'd tell Pete the thirty years worked for him and I'd be happy to copy him.

say: I'd tell people AI is **mostly talk** and the office gets the new toys.
I'd point out the **presses** still need someone to feed them and listen to them.
I'd **stay offline** about it, because posting opinions isn't my thing.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, with a good wage, a year saved and plants nearby.
My real worries stay the old ones: **cheaper countries** and my back at forty.
do: Keep working the **early shift** on the press line as normal.
Keep saving about **a fifth** of each pay packet.
Look at **buying a place** with Lucía in a year or two.
feel: **Calm**, like an ordinary Monday at the plant.
S0.quote: If AI is mostly hype, my biggest worry is still my back at forty, not a computer.
fieldNote: His calm rests on **solid ground**: high pay, a year of savings and many plants nearby.
He has lived through a **lost contract** and saw night-shift workers find jobs fast.
He draws a **firm line** against learning AI tools he sees no use for.
Pete, the **thirty-year setter**, is his model of a good working life.

steps.text: Keep working the early shift on the 400-tonne press line
Put a fifth of every pay packet into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That's more than the first one, but it still sounds slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office that should worry, not us. Scheduling, buying steel, answering the customer: that's all screen work, and that's who this hits first. On the floor I'd joke that the computer still can't free a stuck die at three in the afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd start watching the floor more closely. If the planning goes to software, the next thing the bosses look at is a robot arm loading the press. I'm the guy who loads the press, and loading is the one part a robot does best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep my record clean, no sick days, so if they cut anybody it isn't me. I'd raise my savings from a fifth of my pay to a quarter. And I'd ask Pete to teach me die setting properly, because a setter is the last person they'd get rid of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not scared, just keeping one eye open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI tools. If the plant brought in a tablet telling you what to run, would you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's part of the job, I'd use it, same as I use the clocking machine. I just wouldn't go home and play with it. My cousin Diego asks a chatbot everything, even how to cook rice, and I don't see the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The women in the planning office, honestly, and Marco who does the purchasing. They're decent people and their whole job is the list you just read out. On the floor I'd worry about the packers at the end of the line, because a robot that stacks boxes is already cheap.

say: I'd say the **office** should worry first, since planning and buying are screen work.
I'd joke that a computer still can't free a **stuck die** on the press.
think: I'd expect a **robot arm** to load the press once planning goes to software.
Loading is my main task, and it's the part a **robot** does best.
do: Keep a **clean record** with no sick days so I'm not first to go.
Raise savings from a fifth to **a quarter** of my pay.
Ask Pete to teach me **die setting**, because setters are the last to go.
feel: **Uneasy**, not scared, but keeping one eye on the floor.
S1.quote: I'm the guy who loads the press, and loading is the one part a robot does best.
fieldNote: Publicly he points at the **office**, but privately he sees his own task next.
His plan is old-fashioned: **reliability** and a senior skill rather than new technology.
He'd use AI only when the **job demands** it, never at home.
He worries for **colleagues** in planning, purchasing and packing by name.

steps.text: Keep a clean attendance record with no sick days
Raise savings from a fifth to a quarter of pay
Learn die setting on the presses from Pete, the senior setter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's fast. That's before Lucía and I would even have kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say they've been promising flying cars for fifty years and I'll believe it when I see it. At work I'd say a robot still has to be built, bought and bolted to the floor, and our plant can't even get a new forklift approved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd count. The thinking work goes in 2028, so the office goes first, and then around 2031 the robots come for the floor. That gives me maybe five years in the job I know, and every press plant around here would buy the same robots at the same time, so the other jobs nearby wouldn't save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd drop the idea of a bigger place and keep the money where I can reach it. I'd talk to my uncle Ramón, who has a tiling business, about working Saturdays with him to learn the trade, because people will still want a person in their bathroom. And I'd keep my shifts going as long as they last, every hour of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sick, if I'm honest. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that gap help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps a little and it scares me a little. Three years is enough to learn tiling at weekends, but the whole time I'd watch the office empty out and know the floor is next. It would be like standing on the platform after the train's been announced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which plan or bill goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new flat goes first, straight away. We'd stay in the one I share with my brother, keep the savings untouched and skip the trip to see Lucía's family until I knew what I was doing. A year of pay sounds like a lot until you think it might have to last three years.

say: I'd say people promised **flying cars** too, and I'll believe AGI when I see it.
I'd remind people a robot must be **built, bought and bolted** down first.
think: I'd count about **five years** left before robots reach the press floor.
Every plant nearby would get robots **at once**, so local jobs wouldn't save me.
do: Drop the plan for a **bigger flat** and keep savings within reach.
Work Saturdays with **uncle Ramón** to learn tiling.
Keep working **every shift** on the presses while they last.
S2.quote: A year of pay sounds like a lot until you think it might have to last three years.
fieldNote: His public **disbelief** hides a careful private countdown to 2031.
He sees that **plentiful local jobs** stop mattering when every plant automates together.
He turns to **family** and a trade, not technology or government help.
The **three-year gap** feels to him like waiting for a train he can't stop.

steps.text: Shelve buying a bigger flat with Lucía
Work Saturdays with uncle Ramón to learn tiling
Leave the year of savings untouched as a buffer
Work every shift on the press line until robots arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that I can at least think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing: I'll believe it when the robot's on the floor. But I'd probably say it a bit quieter, because five years is long enough that people would start to see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the thinking AI in 2031 hardly touches me, I don't do much of that. The robots in 2034 do, and I'd be thirty-five. That's young enough to start again, but old enough that I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd do the tiling properly: a weekend course next year and then Saturdays with Ramón for a couple of years. We'd still buy a place, but smaller, and pay it off hard so there's no mortgage when the robots come. Until then I'd stay on the presses, because the money's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a worry with a plan attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would use five years to learn the AI and robot side. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm not a computer guy and I'm not going to pretend at twenty-seven. Somebody has to fix a leaking shower and lay a floor, and I'd rather be that than a guy watching a screen that watches a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for helping people like you through this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families first, then the company. In my dad's day, if somebody lost his job, an uncle found him work. I don't want a cheque from the government for sitting at home; I'd want the company to give us notice and time to train before the robots are bolted down.

say: I'd still say I'll believe it when the **robot's on the floor**.
I'd say it **more quietly**, since five years lets people see it coming.
think: The **thinking AI** in 2031 barely touches my hands-on job.
Robots in 2034 would hit me at **thirty-five**, young enough but unwelcome.
do: Take a **weekend tiling course** next year.
Work Saturdays with Ramón for **two years** to learn the trade.
Buy a **smaller flat** and pay the mortgage off hard.
feel: **Worried**, but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: Somebody has to fix a leaking shower and lay a floor, and I'd rather be that than a guy watching a screen that watches a robot.
fieldNote: He clearly separates **thinking AI**, which spares him, from robots, which don't.
He refuses to move toward **tech work**, choosing a hands-on trade instead.
He puts responsibility on **families and employers**, not state payments.
Five years turns his panic into a **paced plan** with a debt-free home.

steps.text: Take a weekend tiling course next year
Work Saturdays with uncle Ramón for two years
Buy a smaller flat and overpay the mortgage
Stay on the press line while the pay is good

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, and then robots around 2039. I'd be nearly forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and half these predictions never happen. Plenty of the lads at the plant would say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inside, I'd think it's still coming for my job, just later. At nearly forty, maybe with kids in school by then, starting again is harder than at thirty-five, so the extra time is good and bad at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow the same plan but slower: learn tiling over a few years and maybe, by my mid-thirties, go full-time with Ramón or take over part of his business when he retires. We'd buy a house, start a family and keep a year of pay in the bank like always. In the first year I wouldn't change much, I'd mostly wait and see which way it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, maybe a bit anxious. It's far away, but it's still my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said kids might be in school by then. Does that change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. If I had a son starting school around 2036, I'd want him learning a trade that uses his hands and his head, like an electrician. I'd tell my son not to take a job where the machine does the work and you just stand next to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd mostly wait and see, but also learn tiling. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. In the first year I'd mostly wait, because ten years is long and a lot can change. Then if by 2030 the office jobs are really going, I'd stop waiting and go to Ramón.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long and half these predictions never happen.
I'd expect most of the **lads at the plant** to agree with me.
think: The robots still come for my job, just **later**, around 2039.
Starting again near **forty** with kids is harder than at thirty-five.
do: Wait **a year** before changing anything at work.
Learn tiling slowly and maybe **take over** part of Ramón's business.
Buy a house, **start a family** and keep a year of pay saved.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit anxious, because it's distant but still his job.
S4.quote: I'd tell my son not to take a job where the machine does the work and you just stand next to it.
fieldNote: More time doesn't feel safer to him, because he'd be **older** with a family.
He'd **wait first** and set a trigger: office jobs going by 2030.
His advice to a future son shows he quietly sees **his own job** as a dead end.

steps.text: Wait a year before changing anything on the press line
Learn tiling slowly with uncle Ramón over several years
Keep a full year of pay in the bank
Buy a house and start a family as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. Not because of the computers, but because the robots would come by 2031 and every plant around here would buy them at once, so the jobs nearby wouldn't save me. What would help is real notice from the company, a year at least, and apprenticeships in trades like tiling and plumbing that a guy my age can actually get into.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people are proud of. Everyone asks what we'd lose in money, but I'd lose the pallet at two o'clock that I made with my own hands. Nobody pays you for that feeling, but it's why I get up at quarter to five.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks what we'd lose in money, but I'd lose the pallet at two o'clock that I made with my own hands.
portrait: Carlos, 27, runs a **400-tonne press line** making washing machine parts on the early shift.
He is well paid, **saves a year** of wages, and lives with his girlfriend Lucía, a dental nurse.
He is **traditional** and wary of new technology, and never uses AI tools.
He shrugs off the mild scenarios but privately **counts the years** until robots reach the press floor.
His fallback is **family and a trade**: tiling with his uncle Ramón, not tech work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots by 2031 would hit every plant nearby at once.
whatWouldHelp: At least **a year's notice** from the company before robots are installed.
**Apprenticeships** in trades like tiling and plumbing open to people his age.
